lesson.title: Turning Strings Backward: Reversal with Slices
lesson.summary: Extended slice notation with a negative step, s[::-1], reverses a string in a single expression by walking through it from the last character to the first.
lesson.body:
You already know that slice notation lets you pull a piece out of a string using s[start:stop], and that a third number can be added to control the step size, as in s[start:stop:step]. Reversing a string is one of the cleanest demonstrations of why that third value matters. When the step is negative, Python does not walk forward through the string from start to stop, it walks backward, and if you leave start and stop empty while setting the step to -1, you get the entire string traversed from the last character to the first: s[::-1].

It helps to trace exactly what happens with a concrete example. Let word = "python". Writing word[::-1] leaves start and stop blank, which for a step of -1 means "start at the last character and stop after the first one." Python begins at index -1, which is 'n', then -2 which is 'o', then 'h', 't', 'y', and finally 'p'. Concatenating those in the order visited gives 'nohtyp', the reverse of 'python'. Nothing about the original word variable changes; slicing always produces a new string, since strings are immutable, so word still refers to 'python' after this expression runs unless you explicitly reassign it with word = word[::-1].

It is worth understanding why [::-1] works rather than just memorizing it, because the same pattern generalizes. In s[start:stop:step], omitting start and stop does not mean "zero and the length," it means "use whatever default makes sense for the direction of travel." For a positive step, the defaults are the beginning and one past the end. For a negative step, the defaults flip: the beginning becomes the last element and the end becomes one before the first element, which is exactly the range needed to sweep across the whole string in reverse without falling off either edge. You can also reverse only part of a string this way; "hello world"[4::-1] reverses just the first five characters, giving 'olleh', since it starts at index 4, the last letter of "hello", and stops after index 0.

There are other ways to reverse a string, and comparing them clarifies what makes slicing distinctive. The built-in function reversed() returns an iterator, not a string, so reversed("python") needs to be fed to "".join(reversed("python")) to become 'nohtyp' again, an extra step slicing avoids. A manual loop, such as building result = "" and looping for char in word: result = char + result, arrives at the same answer but takes several lines and is noticeably slower for long strings, since string concatenation in a loop creates a new string object on every iteration. Python strings also have no built-in .reverse() method, unlike lists, precisely because reversing in place would mean mutating a string, and strings cannot be mutated at all. The slice [::-1] is the idiomatic choice specifically because it expresses the whole operation as a single, self-contained expression built entirely out of slice notation you already know.
